lines.name: Level: B1+ · Topic: The Costume Shop

lines.text:
Who Do You Want to Be? — A Trip to the Costume Shop

The costume shop on Baker Street is busiest in the weeks before Halloween, school plays, and carnival season. The shelves are packed with outfits, accessories, and everything you need to become someone — or something — else for a day.

The costume racks are organised by character. A pirate costume comes with a hat, an eye patch, a cape, and a toy sword. A princess outfit includes a long dress, a tiara, and a wand. A knight wears armour and carries a shield. A wizard has a long robe, a pointed hat, and a wand. A fairy has wings and a sparkly dress. A cowboy wears a hat, boots, and a vest. An astronaut suit is white and puffy with a helmet. A robot costume is made of silver fabric with blinking lights. A superhero wears a cape and a mask. A ninja is dressed in all black.

The animal section is popular with younger children. Cat ears on a headband, a bunny tail, a lion mane, a dinosaur suit, butterfly wings, a bear onesie, a shark fin hat, a ladybug outfit, a frog hat, and a monkey mask fill the shelves.

Accessories complete every costume. A mask covers the face — full, half, or just the eyes. A wig changes your hair instantly — long, short, curly, straight, any colour. A hat defines the character. A cape adds drama. A sword and a shield make a warrior. A wand makes a wizard. A crown makes a king. A tiara makes a princess. An eye patch makes a pirate.

The makeup section transforms faces. A face paint set includes every colour. A makeup brush applies paint smoothly. A sponge creates texture. Glitter adds sparkle. False eyelashes change the eyes dramatically. Spirit gum — a special adhesive — sticks fake beards, scars, and prosthetics to the skin. Fake blood creates horror effects. Scar wax moulds realistic wounds. A colour palette mixes shades. A mirror sits at every station so customers can see the transformation happening.

Behind the counter, the shop also sells materials for making your own costume. A fabric roll in every colour and texture: sequins for sparkle, feathers for texture, velvet for richness, satin for shine, tulle for volume. Elastic, zippers, and buttons handle the practical details.

The costume shop sells transformation. For a few hours, you can be anyone — a pirate sailing the seas, a fairy in an enchanted forest, or a superhero saving the world. The costume is just fabric, paint, and accessories — but the imagination fills in the rest.

lines.text: 'Dress up as' = wear a costume to be that character: 'She dressed up as a princess.' 'Dress up like' = dress in a similar style (without being): 'She dressed up like a princess' (similar to one). For costumes, 'as' is standard because you ARE pretending to be the character.

lines.text: 'Wear – wore – worn.' Irregular verb — no '-ed' form. 'She wore a mask.' 'They have worn these costumes before.' Common irregular past tenses: 'buy – bought', 'choose – chose', 'put – put' (no change).

lines.text: 'Much' is mainly used in negatives and questions: 'There isn't much choice.' 'Is there much variety?' In positive sentences, use 'a lot of' or 'so much': 'They have a lot of choice.' 'There is so much variety.'

lines.text: '-ed' = how you feel: 'I'm interested.' '-ing' = what causes the feeling: 'The costumes are interesting.' 'I'm excited about the party.' 'The party is exciting.' This -ed/-ing distinction applies to dozens of adjectives: bored/boring, amazed/amazing, confused/confusing.

lines.text: Both 'help + infinitive' and 'help + to infinitive' are correct: 'Help me choose' and 'Help me to choose.' The version without 'to' is more common in spoken English. This is one of the rare cases where both forms are fully accepted.

lines.text: 'Fancy dress' (BrE) = 'costume party' (AmE). In British English, 'fancy dress' specifically means wearing a costume for fun. Confusingly, in American English, 'fancy dress' could mean 'formal/elegant clothing' — opposite meanings!
lines.name: 'Fancy dress' (BrE) = 'costume party' (AmE). In British English, 'fancy dress' specifically means wearing a costume for fun. Confusingly, in American English, 'fancy dress' could mean 'formal/elegant clothing' — opposite meanings!

lines.text: In British English, you 'hire' costumes, cars, and equipment (short-term). You 'rent' a house or flat (long-term). In American English, 'rent' is used for both. 'Let' (BrE) = 'rent out' (AmE): 'She lets her spare room to a student.'

lines.text: 'Traditional dress' or 'national costume' refers to clothing associated with a culture: kimono (Japan), sari (South Asia), thobe (Arabian Peninsula), kilt (Scotland). Avoid 'ethnic costume' — it can sound dismissive. 'Traditional attire' is respectful.

lines.text: In professional theatre, the 'wardrobe department' manages all costumes. The 'costume designer' creates the overall look. 'Wardrobe mistress/master' maintains costumes during the run of a show. A 'quick change' is when an actor changes costume rapidly backstage.
